// Electrical Engineer — Embedded Systems, PCB Design & Software Development

I'm an embedded systems engineer specialised in low-level firmware development, driver design, and hardware/software debugging on STM32 and RP2040 microcontrollers. 01 · About

From bare-metal registers
to high-voltage validation.

I'm an embedded systems engineer specialised in low-level firmware development, driver design, and hardware/software debugging on STM32 and RP2040 microcontrollers. My work spans driver development (GPIO, ADC, Timers, PWM, DMA, interrupts), real-time C/C++ programming, embedded protocols (CAN, CAN FD, LIN, UART, SPI, I2C) and PCB design in KiCad and Altium.

I've contributed to full R&D projects at NGE Automotive — embedded test tools, firmware, DC/DC converters — and to BMS and simulation projects for Stellantis through Capgemini Engineering, where I now sit on the High Voltage Safety Integration team validating powertrain network quality on electric and hybrid vehicles.

Alongside my engineering role, I keep exploring the theory behind the practice — from Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy control of nonlinear thermal systems to FOC and flux-weakening strategies for PMSM traction motors — and share what I learn in short technical write-ups.

Control Theory · Live demo

Nonlinear Thermal System — Takagi–Sugeno Modelling

Full study of a multivariable heat-exchanger: nonlinear 6-state model, linearisation, stability/observability analysis, pole-placement state feedback, a state observer, and a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy reformulation via local linear models.

Protocol Engineering · Test Tooling · NGE Automotive

CAN / CAN-FD / LIN Protocol Test Tool

A physical hardware/software test tool for CAN, CAN-FD and LIN, built around RP2040 State Machines and PIO for precise frame-level timing, with a demonstrator UI for live frame analysis. The driver layer plugs directly into NGE's software scheduler.

CAN FD — frame phasesArbitration → Data → ACK

CAN FD's core idea: arbitration and ACK stay at the slower, detection-safe bit rate, while the data phase switches to a faster clock once the bus is won — exactly the transition the scope captures below.

CAN FD — field layoutSOF → CRC → ACK → EOF

Simplified CAN FD field layout used to validate the tool's frame decoder: start-of-frame, arbitration + control, the variable-length data field, CRC (with stuff-count), CRC delimiter, ACK, and end-of-frame.

Dual-channel scope capture — arbitration phase stepping up into the faster data phase Close-up bit timing — cursor measurement at 588.24 kHz during bit-rate switching
CANCAN FDLINRP2040 PIO / State MachinesFrame decodingBit-rate switching (BRS)
Power Electronics · BMS · Personal project

Battery Management System — Circuit Simulation & PCB Prototype

A ground-up BMS prototype split into four functional blocks — control, charge/discharge, sensing (voltage, current, temperature) and cell balancing — schematically simulated in Proteus ISIS, then laid out as a real PCB in ARES.

// Design notes
Controller
Arduino Nano — Arduino IDE firmware
Charge/discharge
MOSFET-switched charge & discharge stages
Voltage sensing
Per-cell resistive dividers
Current sensing
Shunt resistor + op-amp readout
Balancing
MOSFET bypass balancing per cell state-of-charge
Tools
Proteus ISIS (schematic/sim) → ARES (PCB layout)
Proteus ISIS / ARESArduino NanoPCB designCell balancingV/I/T sensing

The control unit reads per-cell voltage, pack current and temperature, then drives the charge, discharge and balancing MOSFET stages accordingly — the same control/sense/actuate loop used in production BMS architectures, scaled down to a two-cell bench prototype.

Proteus ISIS — charge/discharge stage & per-cell voltage readout (LCD) Proteus ISIS — current & temperature sensing on the same board ARES — final PCB layout routed from the ISIS schematic
Power Electronics · Simulink · Personal project

Three-Phase Rectifier with Buck-Boost DC/DC Regulation

An uncontrolled three-phase rectifier built up in three stages under MATLAB/Simulink: a resistive load to validate baseline AC→DC conversion, an RLE load (inductance + voltage source) to study current/voltage ripple under reactive/back-EMF loading, then a Buck-Boost chopper added downstream to actively regulate the output voltage above or below the rectified level via duty cycle.

// Build stages
Stage 1
3-phase diode bridge, resistive (R) load
Stage 2
RLE load — inductance + back-EMF source added
Stage 3
Buck-Boost chopper inserted for output regulation
Behaviour
Output rises/falls with duty cycle — Buck below, Boost above the rectified level
Tools
MATLAB/Simulink + Simscape Electrical
Simulink / SimscapeThree-phase rectifierBuck-BoostRLE loadDuty-cycle control

Step response of the regulated output as the chopper's duty cycle is swept — a fast transient overshoot settling to a steady DC level, confirming closed-form Buck-Boost behaviour on top of the rectified three-phase input.

Stage 1 — three-phase rectifier, resistive (R) load Stage 2 — RLE load added to study ripple under reactive/back-EMF loading Stage 3 — Buck-Boost chopper integrated for output regulation Output step response — transient overshoot settling to the regulated DC level
Power Electronics · Simulink · Personal project

Three-Phase Voltage Source Inverter — Two Control Strategies

A three-phase VSI modelled and simulated in Simulink under two switching strategies: classic 180° full-wave conduction, and sinusoidal PWM (SPWM) against a high-frequency triangular carrier for finer output control and reduced harmonic content.

// Control strategies
Strategy 1
180° full-wave conduction — each switch on for half a cycle
Strategy 2
Sinusoidal PWM — high-frequency carrier vs. sine reference
Output
Simple & composed (line-to-line) voltages, phase current
Trade-off
PWM trims harmonic content at the cost of switching frequency
Tools
MATLAB/Simulink + Simscape Electrical
Simulink / SimscapeThree-phase VSI180° conductionSPWMHarmonic reduction

Same load, two switching philosophies: 180° conduction gives a stepped six-pulse waveform, while SPWM chops the DC bus at carrier frequency so the filtered/fundamental component approximates a clean sinusoid.

180° control — Simulink model, full-wave conduction 180° control — composed & simple voltage waveforms SPWM control — Simulink model with triangular-carrier PWM stage SPWM control — chopped output tracking the sinusoidal envelope
Motor Control · Simulink · Personal project

Interior PMSM Modelling — Field-Oriented Control in Simulink

A full IPMSM drive built up as cascaded control loops: an outer speed loop generating a torque reference through Maximum Torque Per Ampere (MTPA), an inner dq current loop (PI_Vd / PI_Vq with a polar voltage limiter), position/speed estimation, and an inverter feeding an Interior PMSM plant model.

// Control architecture
Outer loop
Speed control → MTPA reference generation (Iq/Id from torque)
Inner loop
dq current control — separate PI_Vd / PI_Vq regulators
Voltage limiting
Polar limiter on the commanded Vd/Vq before the inverter
Estimation
Position & speed estimation feeding both loops
Plant
Inverter + Interior PMSM (IPMSM) electromechanical model
Tools
MATLAB/Simulink + Simscape Electrical
FOCMTPAPI controldq-framePosition/speed estimationIPMSM plant model

Speed reference steps feed the MTPA block to set the dq current targets; the current loop tracks them through the inverter into the IPMSM plant, closing the loop back through the estimated speed and position feedback.

Top-level architecture — speed/MTPA, current control + estimation, inverter + IPMSM Current control internals — PI_Vd / PI_Vq regulators and polar voltage limiter Inverter + IPMSM internals — motor plant with position/speed feedback Speed response — tracking a series of step reference changes
